user_content:
Record 1 is a name as Dodson & Hilton, *The Complete Royal Families of Ancient Egypt* (2004), print it, without the letter or numeral with which they tell apart women of one name.
Name: Neferuni

The candidates are names from the Thesaurus Linguae Aegyptiae lemma list (January 2018), matched to record 1 by spelling keys; any number of them, or none, may be the same name as record 1. Each candidate is one transliteration, with the modern spellings the TLA gives for each lemma entered under it (descriptions in parentheses or brackets left out). Labels and order are arbitrary.

Candidate C1: Nfr-wn.t
  Lemma 1: German: Nefer-wenet | English: (none)

Candidate C2: Nfr-nw-j
  Lemma 1: German: Nefer-nu-i | English: Nefer-nw-i

Candidate C3: Nfr-jwn.w
  Lemma 1: German: Nefer-iunu | English: (none)

Candidate C4: Nfr.w-Nj.t
  Lemma 1: German: Neferu-Neith | English: (none)

An Egyptian personal name is a sequence of words: names of gods, nouns, adjectives, verbs, prepositions, particles and pronouns. In a TLA transliteration, hyphens and spaces separate words, a dot marks off an ending (such as a feminine .t or a plural .w), and = attaches a suffix pronoun; the translations render the name in modern spelling. A modern spelling such as record 1 renders the same words with vowels added by convention, often written as one word with no separators.

Record 1 and a candidate are the same name when record 1 can be read as the candidate's words, in the same order, by these conventions:
- each consonant sign is rendered by its own letter or letters: ḥ as h; ḫ and ẖ as kh or ch; š as sh; ṯ as tj or t; ḏ as dj or d; z as s; q and ḳ as q or k; every other consonant by its own letter;
- ꜣ and ꜥ are rendered as a vowel or not at all; the weak consonants j (also written ꞽ or i̯), y and w are rendered as i, y, u, w or not at all;
- vowel letters may be added anywhere and stand for no sign;
- apart from what the lines above allow, record 1 may not render a consonant the candidate lacks, nor leave out a consonant the candidate has; the one further omission allowed is a feminine ending t.
Matching consonants are necessary but not enough: the candidate's translations show which words it is made of, and the candidate is a different name when record 1, read as a modern spelling, renders different words (for instance, a different word that happens to share consonants).
Who bore a name is not evidence that two spellings are one name.

How Dodson & Hilton write other names. Each line is another name as Dodson & Hilton print it, with the TLA transliteration an earlier step of this work decided is the same name, or "no TLA name" where it decided that none of that name's candidates is. These are earlier decisions, not ground truth. They show how Dodson & Hilton write names; they do not say which candidate, if any, is record 1's name, and the rules above alone decide whether two spellings are one name.

content.thinking:
Breaking down "Neferuni" phonetically, I'm trying to match it to Nfr-wn.t, treating the feminine ending as dropped and figuring out where the vowel letters fit.

I'm also weighing an alternative reading, Nfr-nw-j, where the order of the n and w sounds would need to be swapped to fit "Neferuni" — mechanically possible but a stretch, so I'm unsure which etymology is actually intended for this 12th dynasty figure.

Trying Neferu-Neith, where Nj.t represents Neith with the feminine ending dropped — though I'm unsure that's the natural way Dodson & Hilton would transliterate the goddess's name. It seems more consistent that Neferuni breaks down as Neferu (matching Nfr.w in known names like Neferuptah) plus ni, so Neferu + Nj(.t) gives Neferu-ni as the pairing for C4.

Actually, thinking about the feminine t-ending more carefully: Neith's name Nt has that t as part of the TLA-treated feminine ending, so dropping it would give "Ni" — not quite matching what's rendered. But I recall a precedent: Anuket's name Dd.t-Ꜥnq.t gets rendered "Anuq" with the t dropped, which supports the idea that D&H do drop this feminine ending in certain compounds.

So maybe Neferu-nit, with the t dropped, becomes "Neferuni" by analogy. I'm also testing whether "wenet" could shorten to "uni" in a similar way, though that stretches the pattern.

I'll rule out the readings involving Iunu and the nw/wn ordering variant, and settle on treating it as Neferu plus Nit.

answer.reasoning: Record 1 divides most naturally as Neferu + ni, the element Neferu being Nfr.w as in the listed Neferu, Neferuptah and Neferure. C4 Nfr.w-Nj.t (Neferu-Neith): nfr.w gives Neferu, and Nj.t gives 'ni' once the feminine t is dropped, which the rules allow. That gives Neferu-Ni(t), and Nit is a recognised rendering of Neith. Dedetanuq (Dd.t-Ꜥnq.t), where the goddess Anuket appears as 'anuq' without its t, supports this reading. Accepted, though with some uncertainty, since Dodson & Hilton might be expected to print 'Neith' in full. C1 Nfr-wn.t (Nefer-wenet): the consonants could be forced (Nefer-un, t dropped), but the final 'i' would then stand for no sign. Record 1 also reads as Neferu-ni rather than Nefer-wen(e)t, so it does not render the word wenet. Rejected. C2 Nfr-nw-j (Nefer-nu-i): the words are nfr + nw + j, with n before w. Record 1 has u before n ('-uni'), so it renders wn rather than nw. That only fits if the u is treated as an inserted vowel and the w is dropped, which does not render 'Nefer-nu-i'. Rejected. C3 Nfr-jwn.w (Nefer-iunu): the words are nfr + Iunu (Heliopolis). Record 1's '-uni' does not render 'iunu', since the final w would have to appear as 'i' and the word would not be recognisable. Rejected.
